very-cold.label: Very cold
very-cold.oneLiner: Long, bitter winters make heating your biggest bill, and summers still need AC.
very-cold.summary: Heating is your biggest bill here: Minneapolis averages 22 nights a year at or below 0°F. Warm air leaking into the attic wastes heat and causes ice dams, and when homes get too cold, a heating breakdown is the usual reason. A good audit seals the attic first, checks that fuel-burning appliances vent safely, and tests for radon.
drivers: Heating dominates: about 7,400 heating degree days a year against 830 cooling degree days, and 72 days that stay below freezing.
Most homes heat with natural gas, and most houses have basements, where rim joists and foundation walls lose heat.
The housing is older: about 6 in 10 Hennepin County homes were built before 1980.
Summers still need cooling: most homes have central AC, and July brings muggy spells.

priorities.title: Seal the attic, then add insulation
priorities.why: Warm air leaking into the attic is a main cause of ice dams. Sealing those leaks before insulating keeps the insulation working. ENERGY STAR suggests an R-value of R60 for an uninsulated attic here.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to find and seal attic bypasses, such as gaps around chimneys, wiring and plumbing, before quoting insulation.

priorities.title: Make sure gas appliances vent safely
priorities.why: Air sealing can make furnaces and water heaters with open flues spill exhaust when fans run, known as backdrafting. A combustion safety test catches it, and you need working CO alarms.
priorities.ask: Ask for a combustion safety test before and after air sealing, with every exhaust fan running.

priorities.title: Test for radon before and after
priorities.why: Hennepin County is in EPA radon Zone 1, the highest-potential zone. The state health department says more than 2 in 5 Minnesota homes have radon levels that pose a significant risk.
priorities.ask: Test before work starts and again after air sealing. Read the two results separately; don't average them.

priorities.title: Seal rim joists; check basement walls for water
priorities.why: Rim joists leak air and heat, and spray foam can seal and insulate them in one step. Fix any water or drainage problems before insulating basement walls.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to inspect the rim joists and look for basement water before writing an insulation plan.

priorities.title: Plan ventilation before deep air sealing
priorities.why: The residential code calls for whole-house mechanical ventilation in homes that test at 5 ACH50 or tighter. An HRV or ERV brings in fresh air while recovering heat.
priorities.ask: Ask what your blower door test result is likely to be after sealing, and whether you'll need an HRV or ERV.

priorities.title: Size any heat pump with Manual J
priorities.why: A cold-climate heat pump can heat your home here, but its size should come from a load calculation. Rules of thumb often oversize systems.
priorities.ask: Ask for a Manual J load calculation and the model's certified heating capacity at 5°F.

tests.why: Measures how leaky your house is, sets air-sealing targets and confirms the result after the work.
tests.when: Heating season, on a calm day. Wind can throw off the numbers.

tests.why: Shows missing insulation, attic bypasses and cold spots. Air leaks stand out when the blower door is running.
tests.when: Winter, early morning or evening. Avoid walls that had sun within about 3 hours, or 8 for masonry.

tests.why: Confirms that open-flue furnaces and water heaters still vent outside with every exhaust fan running.
tests.when: Before and after air sealing, in the heating season with appliances running.

tests.why: Hennepin County is radon Zone 1. A long-term test gives the most accurate result.
tests.when: Heating season, with the house closed up. Retest after air sealing.

tests.why: A Manual J load calculation sizes a new furnace or heat pump to your house instead of a rule of thumb.
tests.when: Before you get equipment quotes, ideally after air sealing and insulation.

upgrades.title: Attic air sealing plus insulation to R60
upgrades.why: Cuts heat loss and is the long-term fix for ice dams. ENERGY STAR says sealing and insulating can save up to 10% on annual energy bills.
upgrades.note: Seal bypasses first; insulation alone won't stop ice dams.

upgrades.title: Rim joist and basement wall insulation
upgrades.why: Closes a large air leak and heat loss path. Closed-cell foam 1.5 inches or thicker also acts as an air barrier.

upgrades.title: Cold-climate heat pump, whole-home or dual-fuel
upgrades.why: Choose a model that meets ENERGY STAR's cold-climate criteria, including a COP of 1.75 or better at 5°F, or one on NEEP's list.
upgrades.note: Keep backup heat for the coldest hours.

upgrades.title: Sealed-combustion or electric replacements
upgrades.why: When an open-flue furnace or water heater is due for replacement, a sealed-combustion or electric unit removes the spillage risk a tighter house creates.
upgrades.note: Plan ventilation at the same time; the change affects how your house breathes.

upgrades.title: Radon mitigation at 4 pCi/L or higher
upgrades.why: EPA recommends fixing your home at 4 pCi/L or more, and considering a fix between 2 and 4.

equipment: You need a cold-climate heat pump for primary heat here. Check its certified performance at 5°F, because HSPF2 ratings are only tested down to 17°F.
Size equipment with a Manual J load calculation, and keep backup heat for the coldest hours: your furnace in a dual-fuel setup, or electric strips.
Federal minimums: 13.4 SEER2 for a split AC, and 14.3 SEER2 with 7.5 HSPF2 for a split heat pump. ENERGY STAR's cold-climate tier for ducted models is 8.1 HSPF2.
A heat pump water heater needs a space that stays between 40°F and 90°F all year, with about 1,000 cubic feet of air. It cools the room it sits in.
health: Radon is the top health item. Hennepin County is EPA Zone 1, and more than 2 in 5 Minnesota homes have levels that pose a significant risk.
Wildfire smoke now reaches Minnesota: 2023 set a record of 22 air-quality alerts covering 52 days. Use MERV 13 filters if your system can handle them, plus a portable air cleaner.
Winter condensation on windows means indoor air is too humid. EPA advises keeping relative humidity below 60%, ideally 30–50%.
In older homes, leave suspected vermiculite or asbestos alone until it's tested. Paid work that disturbs paint in pre-1978 homes must follow EPA lead-safe rules.

avoid.title: Adding attic insulation without sealing bypasses first
avoid.why: Warm air keeps leaking into the attic, so heat loss and ice dams continue.

avoid.title: Installing powered attic ventilators
avoid.why: University of Minnesota Extension advises against them here: they can cause moisture problems and pull air out of your house.

avoid.title: Tightening the house without combustion testing
avoid.why: Open-flue appliances risk backdrafting in a tighter house. Test before and after, and plan ventilation.

avoid.title: Choosing a heat pump by HSPF2 alone
avoid.why: HSPF2 doesn't show how a unit performs at 5°F. Check cold-climate ratings and size it with Manual J.

very-cold.seasonNote: Book in the heating season. Winter gives the best blower door and infrared results, and closed-house conditions suit radon tests. Leave time to retest radon after air sealing.

cold.label: Cold and humid
cold.oneLiner: Heating drives your bills, and older homes lose heat through attics, walls and basements.
cold.summary: Heating is the main bill here, and many homes are decades old, with heat escaping through attics, walls and basements. Older houses may need knob-and-tube wiring, vermiculite or lead paint handled before insulation goes in. Air sealing, attic insulation and a combustion safety test are the core of a good audit.
drivers: Heating dominates: about 5,500 to 6,100 heating degree days a year, against 800 to 1,000 cooling degree days.
Old housing: about 7 to 8 in 10 homes in the core counties were built before 1980, many before 1940.
Heating systems differ: boilers heat about 4 in 10 Boston-area homes, while furnaces dominate around Chicago and Detroit.
Electricity prices vary: about 19 cents/kWh in Illinois, 23 in Michigan and 30 in Massachusetts (August 2026), which shapes heat pump savings.

priorities.title: Seal the attic and wall tops first
priorities.why: Air leaks into the attic waste heat and cause ice dams. Seal them, then insulate. ENERGY STAR suggests an R-value of R60 for an uninsulated attic in this zone.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test with infrared imaging, and a written list of attic bypasses to seal.

priorities.title: Clear old-house hazards before insulating
priorities.why: Live knob-and-tube wiring and vermiculite or asbestos must be dealt with before insulation goes in. Paid work that disturbs paint in pre-1978 homes must follow EPA lead-safe rules.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to check for knob-and-tube wiring, vermiculite and old paint before writing the insulation scope.

priorities.title: Test fuel-burning appliances for safe venting
priorities.why: Air sealing can make open-flue appliances spill exhaust when fans run. A combustion safety test catches backdrafting, and EPA guidance calls for CO testing and alarms.
priorities.ask: Ask for a combustion safety test before and after air sealing, and keep CO alarms working.

priorities.title: Fix basement water, then seal rim joists
priorities.why: Most houses here have basements. Rim joists leak air, and any water problem should be fixed before insulation goes on basement walls.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to check for water entry and to include rim-joist sealing in the plan.

priorities.title: Test for radon, whatever your county's zone
priorities.why: Zones change sharply around these cities. Suffolk and Wayne are Zone 3 and Cook is Zone 2, but Middlesex County, next to Boston, is Zone 1. EPA says test every home.
priorities.ask: Test before work starts and again after air sealing.

priorities.title: Check attic ducts added for central AC
priorities.why: If central AC was added to a radiator-heated house, its ducts may run through the attic. Typical duct systems lose 20–30% of their air through leaks.
priorities.ask: Ask for a duct leakage test, and have any attic ducts sealed and insulated.

tests.why: Measures total air leakage and guides sealing. Pair it with infrared to find bypasses and rim-joist leaks.
tests.when: Winter, on a calm day.

tests.why: Finds missing wall insulation, attic bypasses and rim-joist leaks.
tests.when: Winter, when it's at least 18°F colder outside for about 4 hours. Avoid walls that just had sun.

tests.why: Needed whenever air sealing affects natural-draft boilers, furnaces or water heaters.
tests.when: Before and after air sealing, in the heating season.

tests.why: Radon zones vary from county to county here, so test every home.
tests.when: Heating season, with the house closed up. Retest after air sealing.

tests.why: Vermiculite and asbestos must be handled before insulating, and accredited professionals should take any samples.
tests.when: During the audit walk-through, before the insulation scope is written.

upgrades.title: Air sealing plus attic insulation
upgrades.why: Usually the lowest-cost, highest-impact upgrade in older, heating-dominated homes. ENERGY STAR says sealing and insulating can save up to 10% on annual energy bills.

upgrades.title: Dense-pack insulation for empty walls
upgrades.why: If your older home's walls have no insulation, dense-pack can fill them. Any knob-and-tube wiring has to be cleared first.

upgrades.title: Rim joist and basement wall insulation
upgrades.why: Rim joists are a big, often-missed air leak in basement homes. Seal them, and insulate basement walls once any water problems are fixed.

upgrades.title: Cold-climate heat pumps
upgrades.why: Ductless units suit radiator homes, and ducted ones work where ducts exist. They can displace oil, propane or electric resistance heat. In Massachusetts, Mass Save lists up to $8,500 in 2026 equipment rebates.
upgrades.note: Choose ENERGY STAR cold-climate or NEEP-listed models.

upgrades.title: Sealed-combustion heating or a heat pump water heater
upgrades.why: When it's time to replace, sealed-combustion equipment cuts spillage risk in a tighter house. A heat pump water heater suits a basement that stays between 40°F and 90°F.

equipment: A cold-climate heat pump is strongly advised around Chicago (6.5 nights a year at or below 0°F) and Detroit (3.6), and recommended in Boston (0.6).
Size to the Manual J heating load. A dual-fuel setup, with your furnace as backup, is one way to cover the coldest days.
Federal minimums: 13.4 SEER2 for a split AC, and 14.3 SEER2 with 7.5 HSPF2 for a split heat pump. ENERGY STAR's cold-climate tier for ducted models is 8.1 HSPF2.
Radiator and steam homes usually have no ducts. Ductless mini-splits avoid new attic ductwork; if you add ducts, keep them inside the insulated part of the house.
health: Radon zones change sharply between city and suburban counties, so test every home.
Homes built before 1978 are more likely to have lead paint, and most homes here were built before 1980. Hire a lead-safe certified firm for paid work that disturbs paint.
Wildfire smoke reached the Midwest and Northeast in 2023. MERV 13 filters and portable air cleaners help on smoky days.
Keep relative humidity below 60%. Summer basements often need a dehumidifier, and winter window condensation means the air is too humid.

avoid.title: Insulating over live knob-and-tube wiring
avoid.why: Old wiring, vermiculite and asbestos need to be handled first. Have suspect material sampled by accredited professionals.

avoid.title: Air sealing without combustion and ventilation checks
avoid.why: Open-flue appliances risk backdrafting in a tighter house. At 5 ACH50 or tighter, the code calls for whole-house mechanical ventilation.

avoid.title: Plastic sheeting over fiberglass on basement walls
avoid.why: Interior poly against below-grade walls with fiberglass batts can trap moisture.

avoid.title: Sizing a heat pump on the cooling load
avoid.why: Heating is the bigger load here. Size to the Manual J heating load, not a rule of thumb.

cold.seasonNote: Book in the heating season: cold weather gives the clearest infrared images, and closed-house conditions suit radon tests. Allow time to clear wiring or vermiculite before insulation.

cold-dry.label: Cold and dry
cold-dry.oneLiner: Cold winters, hot but very dry summers, and high radon risk across the Denver area.
cold-dry.summary: Winter heating drives your bills, but summers are hot and very dry. That dry air makes evaporative cooling a real option, and radon is common in Denver-area homes. A good audit pairs air sealing and a combustion safety test with radon testing before and after the work.
drivers: Heating leads: about 5,860 heating degree days a year against 850 cooling degree days, with 156 nights at or below freezing.
Summers are hot but very dry, so cooling is about temperature, not humidity, and evaporative cooling can work.
Most homes heat with gas furnaces, and most houses have basements, so rim joists and basement appliances matter.
Summer heat matters: in a 2023 federal survey, about 1 in 8 Denver-area households were uncomfortably hot for a day or more.

priorities.title: Test for radon before and after work
priorities.why: Denver, Arapahoe and Jefferson counties are EPA radon Zone 1, the highest-potential zone. Larimer County says over half of Colorado homes have elevated levels.
priorities.ask: Test before work and again after air sealing, ideally with a long-term test.

priorities.title: Seal the attic, then insulate
priorities.why: Air sealing comes first, then insulation. ENERGY STAR suggests an R-value of R60 for an uninsulated attic in this zone.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test and a list of attic bypasses to seal before insulation is quoted.

priorities.title: Check that basement appliances vent safely
priorities.why: Tightening a house and running exhaust fans can make open-flue furnaces and water heaters spill exhaust. A combustion safety test checks for backdrafting and carbon monoxide.
priorities.ask: Ask for a combustion safety test before and after air sealing.

priorities.title: Pick a cooling plan that suits dry air
priorities.why: Dry summers make evaporative cooling effective, and a heat pump is the other strong option. Either way, leaky ducts waste the cooling you pay for.
priorities.ask: Ask whether evaporative cooling or a heat pump suits your house, and for a duct leakage test.

priorities.title: Seal rim joists in basement homes
priorities.why: Rim joists are a common air leak in basement homes, and sealing them cuts drafts and heat loss.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to check rim joists with infrared while the blower door runs.

tests.why: Measures air leakage and points to the biggest leaks.
tests.when: Heating season; winter mornings pair best with infrared.

tests.why: Finds attic bypasses, rim-joist leaks and missing insulation.
tests.when: Winter mornings. Strong sun heats south and west walls, so scan from inside and wait 3+ hours after sun.

tests.why: Denver County is radon Zone 1, and a long-term test is the most accurate.
tests.when: Heating season, with the house closed up. Retest after air sealing.

tests.why: Checks natural-draft basement furnaces and water heaters for spillage and carbon monoxide.
tests.when: Before and after air sealing.

tests.why: A Manual J load calculation keeps a new furnace, AC or heat pump from being oversized.
tests.when: Before any HVAC quote.

upgrades.title: Air sealing plus attic insulation
upgrades.why: Heating is the main load here, and ENERGY STAR says sealing and insulating can save up to 10% on annual energy bills.

upgrades.title: Radon mitigation at 4 pCi/L or higher
upgrades.why: EPA recommends fixing your home at 4 pCi/L or more, and considering a fix between 2 and 4.

upgrades.title: Evaporative cooling, direct or two-stage
upgrades.why: In dry air, an evaporative cooler can use about a quarter of the energy of central AC and cost less than half as much to install and run.
upgrades.note: It needs open windows or relief vents, and maintenance at least twice a year.

upgrades.title: Cold-climate heat pump
upgrades.why: Denver averages about 6 nights a year at or below 0°F, so choose a model that meets ENERGY STAR's cold-climate criteria.
upgrades.note: Keep backup heat for the coldest nights.

upgrades.title: Heat pump water heater in the basement
upgrades.why: A basement that stays between 40°F and 90°F suits one, and it cools and dehumidifies the space around it.

equipment: Federal minimums: 13.4 SEER2 for a split AC, and 14.3 SEER2 with 7.5 HSPF2 for a split heat pump.
For heat pumps, choose cold-climate models with verified 5°F performance, size them with Manual J, and keep backup heat.
Evaporative coolers work best when summer humidity is low. They replace the house air every 2–3 minutes, so they need open windows or relief vents.
health: Radon is the headline health risk here. EPA says to test every home, and to fix it at 4 pCi/L or more.
On smoky days, cover evaporative-cooler intakes with MERV 13 filters or run the cooler sparingly, and use MERV 13 in a central system if it can handle it.
Drain an evaporative cooler's pan when it will sit idle for more than a few days, so it can't breed mosquitoes or bacteria such as Legionella.

avoid.title: Running an evaporative cooler with the windows shut
avoid.why: Without relief openings the air has nowhere to go and the cooler can't work. During smoke, filter the intake or limit use.

avoid.title: Skipping the radon retest after air sealing
avoid.why: Sealing changes how air moves through your house, so test again after the work.

avoid.title: Air sealing without combustion testing
avoid.why: Open-flue basement furnaces and water heaters risk backdrafting in a tighter house.

avoid.title: Oversizing the AC
avoid.why: An oversized system short-cycles and wastes energy. Size it with a Manual J load calculation.

cold-dry.seasonNote: Book in the heating season, ideally on a winter morning, for the clearest infrared results and closed-house radon testing. Settle cooling plans before summer.

mixed-humid.label: Mixed-humid
mixed-humid.oneLiner: You pay to heat and to cool, and muggy summers make basements and AC health matter.
mixed-humid.summary: You pay to heat in winter and to cool and dry the air in muggy summers. Many homes are old, with basements that can get damp and lead paint to plan around. A good audit covers air sealing and attic insulation, basement moisture, safe venting of fuel-burning equipment and AC health.
drivers: Two real seasons: about 3,800 to 4,500 heating degree days and 1,300 to 1,700 cooling degree days a year.
Muggy summers: July dew points average 63–67°F, so your AC has to remove moisture as well as heat.
Old housing: in the core cities, the median home was built between 1938 (St. Louis) and 1958 (Washington, DC).
Power is pricey along the Northeast corridor, about 21 to 29 cents/kWh in August 2026, against 16 cents in Missouri.

priorities.title: Seal and insulate for both seasons
priorities.why: Air sealing and attic insulation cut both heating and cooling bills. ENERGY STAR suggests an R-value of R60 for an uninsulated attic in this zone.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test with infrared imaging, and a sealing plan for the attic and top-floor ceilings.

priorities.title: Fix basement water, then seal and dehumidify
priorities.why: Most houses here have basements. Fix water entry first, then seal rim joists and keep summer relative humidity below 60%.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to measure basement humidity and look for water staining before anything is insulated.

priorities.title: Check boilers, furnaces and water heaters vent safely
priorities.why: Open-flue boilers, furnaces and water heaters risk backdrafting once a house is tightened. EPA guidance includes CO testing and alarms.
priorities.ask: Ask for a combustion safety test before and after air sealing, including any oil or steam system.

priorities.title: Plan for lead, asbestos and old wiring
priorities.why: Most homes in these core cities were built before 1980. Paid work that disturbs paint in pre-1978 homes must follow EPA lead-safe rules, and vermiculite or knob-and-tube needs handling before insulation.
priorities.ask: Ask whether the work will disturb paint, and have suspect materials checked before the scope is final.

priorities.title: Test for radon, especially in the suburbs
priorities.why: DC, Philadelphia and New York City are radon Zone 3, but suburban counties such as Montgomery (MD), Fairfax (VA), Bucks and Baltimore County are Zone 1.
priorities.ask: Test before work and again after air sealing, even if your city's zone is low.

priorities.title: Keep the AC healthy and the ducts tight
priorities.why: AC breakdowns are the most common reason homes here get too hot. Typical duct systems lose 20–30% of their air through leaks, and an oversized AC leaves humidity high.
priorities.ask: Ask for a duct leakage test and a check of your AC's size against a Manual J load calculation.

tests.why: Measures air leakage and guides sealing; pair it with infrared to find attic bypasses.
tests.when: Winter is best. Hot afternoons with the AC running can also work.

tests.why: Finds missing insulation and hidden air leaks.
tests.when: Winter, or a hot afternoon with the AC on. Scan from inside and skip walls that just had sun.

tests.why: Checks boilers, furnaces and water heaters for spillage and carbon monoxide in a tightened house.
tests.when: Before and after air sealing.

tests.why: A basement moisture check, with humidity readings and a look for water stains, shows whether it's safe to insulate. Aim for below 60% relative humidity.
tests.when: Mid-summer, when dew points peak.

tests.why: Suburban counties around DC, Baltimore and Philadelphia are Zone 1.
tests.when: With the house closed up, before and after air sealing.

upgrades.title: Air sealing plus attic insulation
upgrades.why: It cuts both heating and cooling loads, and ENERGY STAR says sealing and insulating can save up to 10% on annual energy bills.

upgrades.title: Basement water fixes, rim sealing, dehumidification
upgrades.why: Controls summer basement humidity and mold, and closes a common air leak at the rim joists.

upgrades.title: Duct sealing, or moving ducts inside
upgrades.why: Where ducts run through an unconditioned attic, they can lose 10–45% of the heating and cooling energy they carry. Sealing, insulating or moving them inside cuts that loss.

upgrades.title: Heat pumps, ducted or ductless
upgrades.why: These cities average 0–1 nights a year at or below 0°F, so a standard variable-speed heat pump can carry most hours. Ductless units suit radiator homes.
upgrades.note: A cold-climate heat pump adds margin for cold snaps.

upgrades.title: Heat pump water heater in the basement
upgrades.why: It cools and dehumidifies the space around it, which helps in a muggy basement.

equipment: Federal AC rules differ here: Baltimore and DC follow Southeast rules (14.3 SEER2 for most split ACs), while New York, Philadelphia and St. Louis follow North rules (13.4 SEER2).
Split heat pumps must meet at least 14.3 SEER2 and 7.5 HSPF2. ENERGY STAR models start at 15.2 SEER2 and 7.8 HSPF2.
A cold-climate heat pump is optional, since winters rarely reach 0°F. Still check capacity at 17°F and 5°F for the coldest days.
Size with Manual J. An oversized AC short-cycles and leaves your house cool but clammy.
health: Wildfire smoke: in June 2023, New York City's fine-particle AQI topped 175, a record, and DC had some of its smokiest air in 25 years. Use MERV 13 filters and recirculate.
Heat waves are a serious health risk in these cities, especially in homes without working AC.
Keep basement relative humidity below 60% to limit mold; a dehumidifier helps in summer.
Older homes may hold lead paint and asbestos, and suburban homes may have high radon. Test before work starts.

avoid.title: Plastic vapor barriers on above-grade walls
avoid.why: The code doesn't require interior vapor retarders in this zone, and low-perm layers can trap summer moisture driven inward.

avoid.title: Disturbing lead paint without lead-safe practices
avoid.why: Paid work that disturbs paint in pre-1978 homes must follow EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting rule.

avoid.title: An oversized AC
avoid.why: It cools fast but shuts off before removing moisture, so rooms feel clammy.

avoid.title: Insulating a basement that still takes on water
avoid.why: Fix drainage and leaks first, or the insulation can trap moisture and grow mold.

symptoms: AC breaks down in heat waves

mixed-humid-warm.label: Warm mixed-humid
mixed-humid-warm.oneLiner: Long, muggy summers and short winters; ducts, crawlspaces and humidity drive comfort.
mixed-humid-warm.summary: Summers here are long and muggy, and winters are short but bring regular freezes. Ducts running through hot attics and damp crawlspaces waste energy, and controlling humidity matters as much as temperature. A good audit tests the ducts, checks the attic and crawlspace, and includes a radon test in the Atlanta area.
drivers: Both seasons count: 47–49 days a year reach 90°F, and 36–58 nights fall to 32°F or below.
Very humid summers: July dew points average about 68°F, so your AC must dry the air as well as cool it.
Where ducts run through attics or crawlspaces, leaks and heat loss can waste 10–45% of heating and cooling energy.
Electric heat is common: about half of homes heat with electricity, so heat pump efficiency shows up in winter bills too.

priorities.title: Test and seal ducts in attics and crawlspaces
priorities.why: Leaky or poorly insulated ducts in unconditioned space can waste 10–45% of heating and cooling energy, and typical systems lose 20–30% of their air to leaks.
priorities.ask: Ask for a duct leakage test that measures both total leakage and leakage to outside.

priorities.title: Dry out and close up the crawlspace
priorities.why: EPA's retrofit guidance favors turning vented crawlspaces into sealed, insulated and drained spaces, with a sealed vapor barrier over any dirt floor.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to check crawlspace humidity, wood moisture and standing water, and whether closing it makes sense.

priorities.title: Test for radon
priorities.why: Radon zones vary sharply here: Atlanta's core counties are EPA Zone 1, the highest-potential zone, while Mecklenburg (Charlotte) is Zone 3. EPA says test every home.
priorities.ask: Test before air sealing and again after.

priorities.title: Seal, insulate and shade the attic
priorities.why: ENERGY STAR suggests an R-value of R49 for an uninsulated attic in this zone. A radiant barrier typically trims 8–12% of cooling costs and helps most when ducts run through the attic.
priorities.ask: Ask for attic air sealing first, then insulation, and whether a radiant barrier suits your roof and ducts.

priorities.title: Right-size cooling and control humidity
priorities.why: An oversized AC or heat pump short-cycles and leaves indoor humidity high. Aim to keep relative humidity below 60%.
priorities.ask: Ask for a Manual J load calculation before replacing equipment, and log indoor humidity for a few days.

priorities.title: Check gas furnaces and water heaters vent safely
priorities.why: Where gas equipment remains, open-flue appliances can spill exhaust after air sealing.
priorities.ask: Ask for a combustion safety test if you have gas appliances.

tests.why: Measures total leakage and leakage to outside for ducts in attics and crawlspaces.
tests.when: Any season.

tests.why: Measures whole-house leakage. With infrared, it finds attic bypasses, knee-wall gaps and missing insulation.
tests.when: Winter mornings, when lows average 32–36°F, or hot afternoons with the AC running.

tests.why: A crawlspace check of humidity, wood moisture, standing water and ground cover shows mold risk; indoor humidity logs show whether the AC dries the air.
tests.when: Late summer, when crawlspace humidity peaks.

tests.why: Zones run from 1 to 3 across this region, and EPA says test every home.
tests.when: With the house closed up, before and after air sealing.

tests.why: A Manual J load calculation sizes a new AC or heat pump so it runs long enough to dry the air.
tests.when: Before you get quotes for new equipment.

upgrades.title: Seal and insulate ducts, or move them inside
upgrades.why: Ducts in attics and crawlspaces can waste 10–45% of heating and cooling energy, so this is often the biggest avoidable loss.

upgrades.title: Attic sealing, R49 insulation and a radiant barrier
upgrades.why: Cuts winter heat loss and summer attic heat. A radiant barrier pays off most when ducts run through the attic.

upgrades.title: Closed crawlspace with drainage and dehumidification
upgrades.why: Controls humidity, mold and musty odors under the house.

upgrades.title: Right-sized variable-speed heat pump
upgrades.why: It handles mild winters and long, humid summers. Cold-climate models aren't required here, but check heating capacity on freezing nights.
upgrades.note: Ask how the system controls humidity.

upgrades.title: Heat pump water heater
upgrades.why: It works in a garage or indoor space that stays between 40°F and 90°F, and it cools and dehumidifies that space.

equipment: Southeast rules apply: a new split AC must be at least 14.3 SEER2 (13.8 for the largest sizes), based on installation date.
Split heat pumps must meet at least 14.3 SEER2 and 7.5 HSPF2. ENERGY STAR models start at 15.2 SEER2 and 7.8 HSPF2.
If relative humidity stays above 60% after the system is right-sized, add dehumidification. A dehumidifier won't fix an oversized AC or leaky ducts.
health: Radon can be high even in the South: test every home, before and after air sealing.
Damp crawlspaces can bring mold and musty smells into the house. Keep indoor relative humidity below 60%.
AC failure is the usual reason homes here get uncomfortably hot, so keep your system serviced before summer.

avoid.title: Plastic or vinyl on the inside of exterior walls
avoid.why: The code requires no interior vapor retarder in this zone, and plastic or vinyl wallcovering can trap summer moisture inside the wall.

avoid.title: Venting the crawlspace or leaving bare dirt
avoid.why: Humid summer air vented into a cool crawlspace adds moisture. Cover dirt floors with a sealed vapor barrier.

avoid.title: Buying a bigger AC than you need
avoid.why: Oversized systems short-cycle and leave the house humid.

avoid.title: Skipping radon because 'the South is low'
avoid.why: Radon turns up in all three EPA zones, and some counties here are Zone 1, the highest-potential zone.

symptoms: AC breaks down in heat waves
mixed-humid-warm.seasonNote: Book any time. Late summer shows crawlspace moisture best, and winter mornings or hot afternoons suit infrared. Test radon with the house closed up, before and after air sealing.

hot-humid.label: Hot and humid
hot-humid.regionName: Florida, Texas and the Gulf Coast
hot-humid.oneLiner: Cooling and humidity drive your bills; attic ducts, AC health and outages drive comfort.
hot-humid.summary: Cooling and humidity drive your bills, and in slab homes the ducts often run through a hot attic. Comfort depends on an AC that is sized right, dries the air and keeps running, plus a house that can ride out outages, storms and the occasional hard freeze. A good audit starts with the ducts, the attic and the AC.
drivers: Cooling dominates: about 2,800 to 4,700 cooling degree days a year, and 91 to 124 days at 90°F or more.
Humid air: July dew points average 68–74°F, so your AC has to remove moisture as well as heat.
Most homes sit on slabs, so ducts and the air handler often run through the hottest space in the house, the attic.
Most homes heat with electricity, and long power outages are more common here than nationally.

priorities.title: Fix attic ducts and the air handler
priorities.why: In slab homes this is often the biggest avoidable loss. Return ducts that pull in hot, humid attic air are a classic problem. Check leakage and insulation, and consider bringing ducts inside.
priorities.ask: Ask for a duct leakage test that measures leakage to outside, plus an attic check of duct insulation.

priorities.title: Control humidity, not just temperature
priorities.why: Keep indoor relative humidity below 60%. An oversized AC short-cycles and leaves moisture behind, and AC breakdowns are the top reason homes here get too hot.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to log indoor humidity and compare your AC's size to a Manual J load calculation.

priorities.title: Cut attic heat: insulation and a radiant barrier
priorities.why: ENERGY STAR suggests R30 (zone 1) to R49 (zone 2) for an uninsulated attic. A radiant barrier cuts attic heat flow by about 40%, typically 8–12% of cooling costs.
priorities.ask: Ask whether a radiant barrier fits your roof, and to seal attic air leaks before adding insulation.

priorities.title: Block solar heat at the windows
priorities.why: Single-pane and aluminum-frame windows are still common in this region. Low-SHGC glass, exterior solar screens and shading cut the heat coming in.
priorities.ask: Ask which windows take the most sun, and whether screens or shading would help before replacing windows.

priorities.title: Plan for outages, storms and freezes
priorities.why: Long outages are more common here than nationally, from hurricanes, storms and the occasional hard freeze. A tight, well-insulated house holds its temperature longer.
priorities.ask: Ask how long your house would hold temperature in an outage, and where pipes could freeze in a hard freeze.

priorities.title: Check the pool pump, water heater and radon
priorities.why: About one in six houses in this region has a pool, and its pump is a large, controllable load. Radon turns up in all three EPA zones, so test.
priorities.ask: Ask for pool pump and water heater advice, and test for radon; EPA says every home should be tested.

tests.why: Finds leaks in attic ducts and the air handler, measured as leakage to outside.
tests.when: Any time. Do the attic inspection in the morning, before the attic heats up.

tests.why: Measures whole-house air leakage. With the house depressurized, an infrared scan shows leaks even at small temperature differences.
tests.when: Hot afternoons with the AC on. To image insulation, run the AC a few degrees cooler for about 4 hours first.

tests.why: Logging indoor temperature and humidity for several days shows whether your AC removes moisture. Aim for below 60% relative humidity.
tests.when: Humid spring or fall days, when the AC runs less and humidity tends to climb.

tests.why: A Manual J load calculation checks your AC's size against your house. Some utilities require one for rebates.
tests.when: Before replacing your AC or heat pump.

tests.why: EPA says to test every home, whatever its radon zone.
tests.when: With windows and doors closed, before and after air sealing.

upgrades.title: Seal and insulate ducts, or bring them inside
upgrades.why: Options include a sealed attic or burying ducts in insulation. In humid climates, buried ducts must first be encapsulated in closed-cell foam to prevent condensation.
upgrades.note: A sealed attic needs a way to remove moisture.

upgrades.title: Right-sized variable-speed AC or heat pump
upgrades.why: Sized with Manual J and Manual S, it runs longer, gentler cycles that pull more moisture from the air.
upgrades.note: Add a dehumidifier only if humidity stays above 60% afterward.

upgrades.title: Attic insulation plus a radiant barrier
upgrades.why: Attic heat drives your cooling load and heats any ducts up there. A radiant barrier cuts attic heat flow about 40%.
upgrades.note: Install foil at the roof deck or rafters, not on the attic floor, where dust ruins it.

upgrades.title: Solar control at the windows
upgrades.why: Low-SHGC glass, exterior solar screens and shading cut solar heat gain. Some utility programs, such as CPS Energy's Casa Verde, fund solar screens.

upgrades.title: Heat pump water heater in the garage
upgrades.why: It cools and dehumidifies the space around it.
upgrades.note: It needs a space that stays between 40°F and 90°F.

equipment: Southeast rules: a new split AC must be at least 14.3 SEER2 (13.8 for the largest sizes), based on installation date. EER2 shows efficiency on the hottest afternoons.
Heating loads are small, so a heat pump or AC with strip heat covers most winters. Where hard freezes come, check the heat pump's output at 17°F and size the backup heat for a multi-day cold snap.
Size with Manual J and Manual S, not a rule of thumb. Oversized systems short-cycle and leave the house humid.
Avoid exhaust-only ventilation: it depressurizes the house and pulls in humid outdoor air. Balanced ventilation, such as an ERV, avoids that.
health: Mold and dust mites thrive in humid air. Keep indoor relative humidity below 60%, ideally 30–50%.
Long outages in summer heat are a health risk. Keep portable generators outside, away from windows and doors, because their exhaust contains carbon monoxide.
In flood-prone areas, ask the auditor about where your equipment sits and any signs of water intrusion.

avoid.title: Plastic or vinyl wallpaper on exterior walls
avoid.why: On the inside of exterior walls, plastic or vinyl wallpaper traps moisture that humid outdoor air drives into the wall.

avoid.title: Oversized AC or rule-of-thumb sizing
avoid.why: Short cycles leave humidity behind. Insist on a Manual J load calculation.

avoid.title: Burying attic ducts without encapsulating them
avoid.why: In humid climates, ducts buried in insulation without closed-cell foam can sweat and drip.

avoid.title: Sealing the attic without moisture removal
avoid.why: A sealed attic brings ducts inside the envelope, but it needs a way to remove moisture.

symptoms: AC breaks down in heat waves
Too hot or cold during outages
hot-humid.seasonNote: Book in spring, before peak heat, so fixes are done by summer. Hot afternoons suit infrared, and humid spring or fall days show whether your AC dries the air.

hot-dry.label: Hot and dry
hot-dry.oneLiner: Months of extreme heat make AC your biggest bill and a safety system, too.
hot-dry.summary: Cooling is your biggest bill, and in extreme heat your AC is also a safety system. Ducts and air handlers often sit in the attic, the hottest place in the house, so leaks there waste a lot of cooling. A good audit checks the AC's health and size, tests and seals the ducts, and cuts attic and window heat.
drivers: Extreme, long heat: 100°F days come by the dozens each summer (Phoenix averages 111 a year).
Dry heat: summer dew points are low, so cooling is mostly about temperature. The monsoon raises humidity in late summer.
Most homes sit on slabs, so ducts and air handlers often run through the attic, the hottest space in the house.
Power prices differ: about 15 cents/kWh in Arizona against about 30 cents in California (August 2026), so the same cooling costs about twice as much in California.

priorities.title: Keep your AC reliable and right-sized
priorities.why: A working AC is a safety system here. In Maricopa County's 2024 indoor heat deaths, 88% of homes had an AC, but 70% of those units weren't working.
priorities.ask: Ask for an AC performance check and a Manual J comparison before you repair or replace your system.

priorities.title: Seal and insulate attic ducts
priorities.why: Ducts in an unconditioned attic can lose 10–45% of the cooling they carry, and typical systems lose 20–30% of their air to leaks.
priorities.ask: Ask for a duct leakage test that measures leakage to outside, and a check of the attic air handler.

priorities.title: Cut attic heat gain
priorities.why: ENERGY STAR suggests an R-value of R49 for an uninsulated attic in zones 2 and 3. A radiant barrier typically saves 8–12% of cooling costs and keeps attic ducts cooler.
priorities.ask: Ask whether a radiant barrier at the roof deck makes sense, and to seal attic leaks before insulating.

priorities.title: Tame west sun and old windows
priorities.why: Single-pane glass is still common in this region. Shading, solar screens and low-SHGC glass cut the heat coming in.
priorities.ask: Ask which windows take the hottest sun, and whether screens or shading should come before new windows.

priorities.title: Keep dust and smoke out
priorities.why: Air leaks let in desert dust and, on smoky days, wildfire smoke. Sealing leaks and using MERV 13 filters keep more of it outside.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test to find leakage paths, and whether your system can take a MERV 13 filter.

priorities.title: Check the pool pump and water heater
priorities.why: About one in six houses in this region has a pool. Pool pumps and water heating are large loads you can control.
priorities.ask: Ask for pool pump run-time and water heater recommendations; your bills can show how big these loads are.

tests.why: With a big indoor-outdoor temperature difference, missing insulation and air leaks show up clearly.
tests.when: Summer afternoons with the AC running. Scan from inside; sun-baked outside walls give misleading readings for hours.

tests.why: Finds leaks in attic ducts and the air handler.
tests.when: Early morning, before the attic gets too hot to work in safely.

tests.why: Measures total air leakage and finds the paths dust and smoke take into your house.
tests.when: Any season.

tests.why: A Manual J load calculation checks whether your AC is the right size before you repair or replace it.
tests.when: Cooling season, before any replacement.

upgrades.title: Duct sealing, plus insulation or buried ducts
upgrades.why: In dry climates, burying ducts in attic insulation works without the condensation worries of humid areas.

upgrades.title: Attic insulation plus a roof-deck radiant barrier
upgrades.why: A radiant barrier cuts heat flow from the attic into the house by about 40%, typically 8–12% of cooling costs, and keeps attic ducts cooler.
upgrades.note: Install foil at the roof deck or rafters, never on the attic floor.

upgrades.title: High-EER2 AC or heat pump
upgrades.why: EER2 measures efficiency at peak heat, which is why Southwest rules set an EER2 minimum. A heat pump also covers your small heating load.

upgrades.title: Evaporative or two-stage cooling, where it fits
upgrades.why: An evaporative cooler can use about a quarter of the energy of central AC. It works less well as humidity rises, such as during the monsoon.
upgrades.note: It needs relief vents or open windows, and regular maintenance.

upgrades.title: Shade screens and window shading
upgrades.why: Solar screens and shading cut heat through older glass. SRP, for example, rebates professionally installed shade screens.

equipment: Southwest rules: most new split ACs need at least 14.3 SEER2 and 11.7 EER2 (9.8 EER2 if rated 15.2 SEER2 or higher). Packaged ACs need at least 10.6 EER2.
Heat pumps suit this climate: heating loads are small, and about a third of Phoenix-area homes already heat with one.
Direct evaporative coolers drop supply air 15–40°F but add humidity. Indirect and indirect/direct units cool without adding moisture.
Size with a Manual J load calculation; oversized units short-cycle.
health: Heat illness is the main risk when AC fails. Keep your system maintained and have a backup plan for cooling.
On smoky or dusty days, use MERV 13 filters, recirculate indoor air and filter any evaporative cooler intake.
Drain an idle evaporative cooler's pan so it can't breed mosquitoes or bacteria such as Legionella.
Radon turns up in desert homes too. EPA says to test every home.

avoid.title: Buying an AC on SEER2 alone
avoid.why: EER2 shows efficiency at peak heat, and Southwest rules set a minimum for it.

avoid.title: Running an evaporative cooler with the windows shut
avoid.why: Without relief openings it can't work. In humid or smoky spells, adjust use or filter the intake.

avoid.title: Laying radiant barrier foil on the attic floor
avoid.why: Dust settles on it and ruins its effect. Install it at the roof deck or rafters.

avoid.title: An oversized AC
avoid.why: Bigger isn't better: oversized units short-cycle and run less efficiently.

hot-dry.seasonNote: Get the AC checked in spring, before triple-digit heat. Summer afternoons give the clearest infrared images, but attic and duct work belongs in the early morning.

mild-coastal.label: Mild coastal
mild-coastal.oneLiner: Small loads and high power prices, plus heat waves in homes built without AC.
mild-coastal.summary: Your heating and cooling loads are small, but California electricity costs far more than the national average, so waste still adds up. Many homes have no AC, and many older ones heat with wall or floor furnaces, so heat-wave planning and safe venting matter most. A good audit seals and insulates the attic, tests fuel-burning equipment and sizes any cooling for heat waves without oversizing.
drivers: Small loads: the coastal airports log only about 200 to 900 cooling degree days and 1,000 to 2,500 heating degree days a year.
High prices: California electricity averaged about 30 cents/kWh in August 2026, against about 18 cents nationally.
Many homes lack AC: about half of San Francisco-area homes and nearly 1 in 5 Los Angeles-area homes have none.
Inland is different: hotter valleys behave like the Hot and dry climate, with many more 90°F days than the coast.

priorities.title: Seal and insulate the attic
priorities.why: ENERGY STAR suggests an R-value of R49 for an uninsulated attic in this zone. A well-insulated attic helps in winter and keeps homes without AC cooler in heat waves.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test with infrared imaging, and a list of ceiling leaks to seal before insulating.

priorities.title: Check wall furnaces and water heaters vent safely
priorities.why: Wall and floor furnaces are common in older Los Angeles and San Francisco homes. Check them for spillage and carbon monoxide, especially before air sealing.
priorities.ask: Ask for a combustion safety test before and after air sealing, and keep CO alarms working.

priorities.title: Prepare for heat waves without oversizing
priorities.why: Many homes lack AC, and the top reason people here give for being too hot is not enough cooling capacity. A right-sized heat pump adds efficient cooling and can replace a wall furnace.
priorities.ask: Ask for a Manual J load calculation that sizes cooling for heat waves, not a rule of thumb.

priorities.title: Check ducts in attics and under floors
priorities.why: Ducts here often run through attics or crawlspaces under raised floors, and typical systems lose 20–30% of their air through leaks.
priorities.ask: Ask for a duct leakage test if you have a forced-air furnace.

priorities.title: Brace the water heater for earthquakes
priorities.why: California law requires water heaters to be braced, anchored or strapped, and Los Angeles and San Francisco face some of the highest earthquake risk in the US.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to check the water heater's strapping and gas connector.

tests.why: Measures air leakage and guides attic and ceiling sealing.
tests.when: Any season; pair it with infrared on a winter morning.

tests.why: Finds missing insulation and ceiling bypasses.
tests.when: Winter mornings with the heat on, when it's about 18–24°F cooler outside. Coastal summers rarely give enough contrast.

tests.why: Checks wall furnaces, floor furnaces and water heaters for spillage and carbon monoxide.
tests.when: Heating season, before and after air sealing.

tests.why: Finds leaks in ducts that run through attics or under raised floors.
tests.when: Any season.

tests.why: A Manual J load calculation sizes a heat pump for heat waves without oversizing it.
tests.when: Before you buy cooling or a heat pump.

upgrades.title: Air sealing plus attic insulation
upgrades.why: In Los Angeles, inadequate insulation is one of the top reasons people give for being too cold. ENERGY STAR says sealing and insulating can save up to 10% on annual energy bills.

upgrades.title: Heat pump to replace a wall furnace
upgrades.why: A ducted or ductless heat pump adds cooling for heat waves and heats efficiently. Cold-climate models aren't needed: the coastal airports almost never freeze.

upgrades.title: Duct sealing
upgrades.why: Typical systems lose 20–30% of their air through leaks, and ducts here often run through attics or under raised floors.

upgrades.title: Heat pump water heater
upgrades.why: It moves heat instead of making it, and it needs a space that stays between 40°F and 90°F.

upgrades.title: Attic heat control for inland homes
upgrades.why: In hotter inland neighborhoods, a radiant barrier cuts attic heat during heat waves. At the cool coast, it does much less.

equipment: Southwest rules apply statewide: a new split AC needs at least 14.3 SEER2 plus an EER2 minimum, based on installation date.
A standard heat pump is enough here. The coastal airports average almost no nights at or below freezing, so you don't need a cold-climate heat pump.
Size cooling for heat waves with a Manual J load calculation, without oversizing.
health: Wildfire smoke: on smoky days, use MERV 13 filters, recirculate indoor air and run a portable air cleaner.
Wall furnaces and water heaters can produce carbon monoxide if they vent poorly. Keep CO alarms working.
Heat waves are a health risk in homes without AC. Plan how you'll keep at least one room cool.
Radon turns up in every EPA zone, so test. In pre-1978 homes, use lead-safe certified firms for paint work.

avoid.title: Desert-style oversized cooling at the coast
avoid.why: Your loads are small. An oversized system costs more and short-cycles, and you don't need cold-climate heating either.

avoid.title: Tightening a house with wall furnaces, untested

marine.label: Marine
marine.oneLiner: A long, damp heating season, plus summer heat waves many homes aren't built for.
marine.summary: Your heating season is long and damp, and many homes heat with electric baseboards. Summers are usually mild, but the 2021 heat dome showed how many homes have no way to cool. A heat pump can solve both, and a good audit also checks the crawlspace, the attic and ventilation.
drivers: Heating leads: about 4,100 to 4,400 heating degree days a year, but only 265 to 510 cooling degree days.
Electric heat is common: about half of homes heat with electricity, much of it with baseboard heaters.
Heat waves are new: the June 2021 heat dome set all-time records across the region, and many homes have no AC.
Most houses sit over crawlspaces, so ground moisture, floor insulation and crawlspace ducts matter.

priorities.title: Switch to a heat pump that also cools
priorities.why: Homes with baseboard heat or no AC gain the most. One heat pump replaces resistance heat and covers heat waves.
priorities.ask: Ask for a Manual J load calculation that sizes for winter heating and checks summer cooling capacity.

priorities.title: Fix the crawlspace: drainage, ground cover, insulation
priorities.why: Fix drainage first, then lay a sealed vapor barrier over the dirt. ENERGY STAR suggests an R-value of R30 for floor insulation in this zone.
priorities.ask: Ask the auditor to check crawlspace moisture, the ground cover and any ducts down there.

priorities.title: Seal and insulate the attic
priorities.why: A long heating season makes this a core upgrade. ENERGY STAR suggests R60 for an uninsulated attic in this zone.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test with infrared imaging to find attic bypasses before insulating.

priorities.title: Plan ventilation for a long damp season
priorities.why: If air sealing brings your house to 5 ACH50 or tighter, the code calls for whole-house mechanical ventilation, such as an HRV or ERV.
priorities.ask: Ask what your blower door test result will be after sealing, and how the house will get fresh air.

priorities.title: Test radon and gas appliance venting
priorities.why: EPA says every home should be tested for radon. In homes with gas heat, open-flue appliances can spill exhaust after air sealing.
priorities.ask: Ask for a radon test and, if you have gas, a combustion safety test before and after sealing.

tests.why: Measures air leakage; pair it with infrared to find attic bypasses and missing wall and floor insulation.
tests.when: Winter mornings, when it's about 30°F colder outside than in. Summer is usually too mild for infrared.

tests.why: A crawlspace check of moisture, ground cover and duct condition shows whether floor insulation or closing the crawlspace is safe.
tests.when: Late winter or spring, when crawlspaces are wettest.

tests.why: Crawlspace and attic ducts leak and can pull in damp air.
tests.when: Any season.

upgrades.title: Heat pumps replacing baseboard or old furnaces
upgrades.why: Ductless or ducted, a heat pump gives efficient heat plus cooling for heat waves.

upgrades.title: Air sealing plus attic insulation
upgrades.why: A long, mild heating season rewards it, and ENERGY STAR says sealing and insulating can save up to 10% on annual energy bills.

upgrades.title: Crawlspace vapor barrier and floor insulation
upgrades.why: Most homes sit over crawlspaces. Fix drainage, lay a sealed ground cover, then insulate the floor to R30, or close the crawlspace.

upgrades.title: Duct sealing
upgrades.why: Crawlspace ducts leak and can draw in damp air. Typical systems lose 20–30% of their air through leaks.

upgrades.title: Heat pump water heater
upgrades.why: Mild garages and basements suit them, and they need a space that stays between 40°F and 90°F.

equipment: North rules: at least 13.4 SEER2 for a split AC, and 14.3 SEER2 with 7.5 HSPF2 for a split heat pump.
Winters rarely reach 0°F, so a standard variable-speed heat pump handles most hours. A cold-climate heat pump adds margin for cold snaps and ice storms.
Size to the Manual J heating load, but confirm the system has enough cooling capacity for heat-dome events.
health: Wildfire smoke can reach hazardous levels: use MERV 13 filters, recirculate indoor air and run portable air cleaners.
Winter condensation and mold: keep indoor relative humidity below 60%, ideally 30–50%.
Heat waves are a health risk in homes without AC.
Radon turns up in every EPA zone. EPA says to test every home.

avoid.title: Insulating crawlspace floors before fixing moisture
avoid.why: Without a ground cover and moisture control, new floor insulation can stay damp and grow mold.

avoid.title: Air sealing without a ventilation plan
avoid.why: A tight house needs fresh air, especially in a long damp season. At 5 ACH50 or tighter, the code calls for mechanical ventilation.

avoid.title: Sizing a heat pump for heating only
avoid.why: Recent heat waves mean you need enough cooling capacity, too.

avoid.title: Ignoring vapor-retarder rules in this zone
avoid.why: The code sets specific vapor-retarder rules for this marine zone. Ask how any wall upgrade will meet them.
